clinicalPearls: A distinct subset of gastrointestinal stromal tumours lacking KIT and PDGFRA mutations, driven instead by loss of succinate dehydrogenase complex function (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC or SDHD)
Almost always arises in the stomach and shows a characteristic multinodular or plexiform growth pattern with epithelioid or mixed cytology
Predominantly affects children, adolescents and young adults, with a female predominance, and is the typical GIST of the young
Loss of SDHB immunohistochemical staining is the unifying diagnostic feature regardless of which subunit gene is affected; loss of SDHA staining specifically indicates an SDHA mutation
Frequently harbours germline SDH mutations, so identification should prompt genetic counselling and evaluation for hereditary paraganglioma-phaeochromocytoma syndromes
Associated with the Carney triad (gastric GIST, paraganglioma and pulmonary chondroma) and the Carney-Stratakis dyad (GIST and paraganglioma with germline SDH mutation)
Behaves differently from conventional GIST, with frequent lymph node metastasis yet often an indolent, protracted course even with metastatic disease
Characteristically resistant to standard imatinib therapy because it does not depend on KIT or PDGFRA signalling
reference.pathophysiology: SDH-deficient GIST results from loss of function of the mitochondrial succinate dehydrogenase complex, through germline or somatic mutation of one of its subunit genes or, in some cases, epigenetic silencing of SDHC. Failure of this enzyme causes accumulation of succinate, which inhibits prolyl hydroxylases and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors, producing a pseudohypoxic state that drives angiogenesis and tumour growth. Because the disease is independent of KIT and PDGFRA activation, it forms a biologically separate group with distinct morphology, natural history and treatment response.
additionalDifferentials: Conventional KIT or PDGFRA-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumour
additionalInvestigations: SDHB immunohistochemistry, with SDHA staining to identify SDHA-mutant cases
Mutational testing confirming absence of KIT and PDGFRA mutations
Germline SDH gene testing with referral for genetic counselling
Screening for paraganglioma and phaeochromocytoma, including biochemical catecholamine studies and imaging
Evaluation for pulmonary chondroma when a Carney triad is suspected
Cross-sectional imaging to assess multifocality, nodal and hepatic metastases
redFlags: Young patient with a gastric mass and multifocal or nodal disease
Coexisting paraganglioma or phaeochromocytoma suggesting a hereditary syndrome
Family history of paraganglioma, phaeochromocytoma or GIST
Progressive metastatic disease despite the typically indolent course
Symptomatic gastrointestinal bleeding from an ulcerating gastric tumour
reference.prognosis: SDH-deficient GIST tends to follow an indolent, protracted course, and patients may live for many years even with lymph node or liver metastases; conventional tyrosine kinase inhibitors are largely ineffective, so complete surgical resection is the mainstay, and lifelong surveillance is needed because of multifocality and the risk of associated syndromic tumours.
pitfalls: Assuming all GISTs will respond to imatinib and overlooking the wild-type, SDH-deficient subset
Not performing SDHB immunohistochemistry in a young patient with a gastric GIST
Failing to recognise the hereditary implications and omitting germline testing and family screening
Applying conventional GIST risk-stratification schemes, which do not reliably predict behaviour in this subset
Interpreting nodal metastasis as necessarily indicating a poor outcome
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Digestive System Tumours
